title: When followers lag: read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix
goal: By the end, you can draw the three surprises a lagging follower causes (your own change missing, data going back in time, an effect shown before its cause) as moments on one log, cause the first on a real PostgreSQL standby, and prevent each with a position the reader carries, a fixed follower per user or one shared log, knowing what each fix costs.
opening:
Picture a café owner at closing time. A customer's coffee was charged twice, so she opens the payments app on her phone and taps Refund. The app says "Refund sent". She reloads the page to check, and the refund isn't in the list. So she taps Refund again.

The first refund worked. The page was read from a copy of the database that hadn't received it yet, a few hundred milliseconds behind. It's easy to trust the screen, because the screen is all she can see. And it's easy for the people who built the app to miss this: on a quiet test computer, the copies are a millisecond behind, and every reload looks right.

In Replication logs, every follower ended up with exactly the leader's data, only later. In this lesson, we'll measure how much later, cause three different surprises with that delay, and fix each one by making the reader carry a position in the log. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The café owner's refund page reads from a follower that's 300 ms behind the leader. Right after she asks for a refund, the page reloads, shows no refund, and she taps Refund again. Which change fixes this for every shop owner at the lowest cost?
options: Make the leader wait for every follower before it says OK
Remember the log position of each user's last change, and read from a follower only once it has reached that position, otherwise from the leader
Add more followers, so each one has less work and falls less far behind
Save each page for a second, so reloads are faster
warmup.why: Only this owner's own change is missing, so only her reads need to wait or go to the leader, and only until the follower catches up. Waiting for every follower would fix it too, by making every payment wait for the slowest follower. More followers don't put a limit on how far behind each one can be. A saved page shows an even older answer. (The second refund should also be refused by a key that makes a repeated request harmless, as in Rate limiting and idempotency keys. That protects the money, not the screen.)

sections.h: Followers are behind, and nobody promises by how much
sections.body:
Let's look at where the café owner's page gets its data. Every shop owner has pages like hers, of payments and refunds, and together they ask a lot of questions. So the company's program sends 90% of those reads to three followers, and the leader keeps its processor for recording card payments. One leader, many followers showed why those followers must be asynchronous: if the leader waited for all three, the slowest would set the speed of every payment.

So the pages read the past. Usually it's a few milliseconds old. During a burst of writes, the replay of one huge change or a slow network link, it can be seconds or minutes old. A long read on a follower can even hold up its replay (lesson 4). Nothing in the design puts a limit on it.

Picture the club's notebook again, with photocopies of each new page posted to other towns. Each town's copy is right as of the last letter it got. If the club stopped writing, every town would catch up in a few days and hold the same pages.

Followers work the same way. If the writes stopped, every follower would catch up and agree with the leader. That's all **eventual consistency** promises: the copies agree in the end, and "the end" comes with no number. Asynchronous followers of PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle, three databases that store data in tables, are eventually consistent too. That's exactly what people say about NoSQL databases, the ones such as MongoDB that store data in other shapes.

Keep lesson 1's picture: one log with positions, and each follower at some position in it. Add one rule: a read on a follower returns the data as of that follower's position. **Lag** is the distance between the leader's position and the follower's, and every database will tell you what it is:

- PostgreSQL, on the leader: `pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn)` in the report `pg_stat_replication` gives it in bytes, and `replay_lag` gives it as time.
- MySQL: `Seconds_Behind_Source` in `SHOW REPLICA STATUS`, an estimate in seconds.
- MongoDB: `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()` on its command line, for each follower.
- Redis, a database that keeps its data in memory: the leader's `master_repl_offset` minus each follower's offset, in `INFO replication`.

Data that's older than the newest is called stale, and on its own it's often fine. A sales total that's two seconds old surprises nobody. Trouble starts when a reader already knows about something newer than the follower they're reading. In the club's terms, an old copy only surprises someone who has seen a newer page.

Each of this lesson's three surprises is a read served at a position behind something the reader has already done or seen. And each fix is the same move in a different form: **the reader carries a position, and refuses to read below it.**

The analogy breaks in one place. A town's copy has a date on its last page, so a reader can tell how old it is. A follower's answer carries no date at all, unless the program asks for the follower's position.

The first surprise is the café owner's: her own refund, missing.

try.title: Positions over time
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the first command below. It runs on pretend time, so every run gives the same result. A payment is captured every 100 ms until 2,000 ms, follower r1 is 20 ms behind the leader, and r2 is 900 ms behind. It prints each machine's log position, and whether r2 can show pay-15 yet.
Predict when r2 first shows pay-15, which the leader committed at 1,500 ms. Then run the second command, where r2 is 2,500 ms behind, and say how long "eventually" is now.
try.expect:
```text
a payment captured every 100 ms; r1 is 20 ms behind, r2 is 900 ms behind
    time   leader         r1         r2             pay-15 on r2
  500 ms        5          4          0                not there
 1000 ms       10          9          1                not there
 1500 ms       15         14          6                not there
 2000 ms       20         19         11                not there
 2500 ms       20         20         16                 captured
 3000 ms       20         20         20                 captured
once the writes stop at 2,000 ms, both followers converge: that is all "eventually consistent" promises
```

r2 shows pay-15 from 2,400 ms, 900 ms after the commit. A lag in time becomes a lag in positions that depends on how fast writes arrive: 900 ms behind is 9 payments at this rate, and would be 9,000 at a busy one. With a 2,500 ms lag, r2 is still at 0 at 2,500 ms and at 5 at 3,000 ms. It reaches 20 at 4,500 ms, after the table ends and long after the last write.

sections.h: Seeing your own changes: carry the position of your last write
sections.body:
Here's the café owner's evening on the lab's clock. At 1,000 ms she asks for a refund of pay-41. The leader commits it at position 2. At 1,010 ms her page reloads, and the load balancer, a program that spreads reads across the followers, sends the question to follower r1. It's 300 ms behind and still at position 0, so the refund list is empty. She taps Refund again.

An idempotency key stops the second refund in the database. (That's a key the app sends with each request, so that the database refuses a repeat. Rate limiting and idempotency keys, in the Caching track, builds one.) But the screen was wrong, and the café owner's call to the support line is real.

The promise she needs is called **read-your-writes**, or read-after-write: after you change something, your own reads always show the change. It says nothing about other people's reads. There are four ways to get it, from blunt to precise.

1. Read anything the user can change from the leader: their own refunds, their settings. It's simple and correct, until most pages show the user's own data and the leader takes most reads again.
2. Read from the leader for a fixed time after each of the user's changes, say one minute. This one is a trap. It passes every test, because lag in tests is milliseconds. Then a follower restarts and replays for six minutes, and every user who changed something in that window sees their change vanish.
3. Carry the position. When a change commits, the app saves its log position as a token in the user's session, the app's memory of one signed-in user. Before reading on a follower, the router (the part of the app that picks a machine for each read) compares the follower's position with the token. At or past it: read there. Behind it: wait a little, or go to the leader.
4. Make the commit wait. PostgreSQL's `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` returns only once a standby has applied the change (lesson 4). Every read there is fresh, and every commit pays for it.

On PostgreSQL, option 3's token is `pg_current_wal_lsn()`, read right after the commit, and the check on the standby is `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= token`. (An LSN is PostgreSQL's name for a log position. PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds a `WAIT FOR LSN` command for the waiting.) MySQL gives every transaction an id, a GTID. Its token is the set of those ids, checked with `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET`. MongoDB builds it in. A causally consistent session remembers the time of its last write and sends it with each read as `afterClusterTime`. A follower then waits until it has applied that far. MongoDB's manual promises this only when reads and writes both use its `majority` setting.

Option 3 is usually the right one. It sends to the leader only the reads that would be wrong, and it measures freshness by position, not by the clock. It brings two costs. The token must live where every request of that user can find it. A cookie, the small note a website keeps in one browser, works for one browser. A shop owner who refunds on her phone and checks on her laptop needs the token kept by the server, under her account. And a follower that never catches up (paused, broken, far behind) must not hold a read forever, so limit the wait and fall back to the leader.

**Compare positions, not clocks.**

Her own refund now always shows. Next, someone who changed nothing at all watches a payment go back in time.

Making everyone see every change at once is a far stronger promise, linearizability, which the Consistency and consensus track takes on.

try.title: Lose your own refund on a real standby, then check the position
steps: Start the leader and its standby from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait`. Open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line program, on each, in two terminal windows: `docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course` and `docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course`.
Run the session below, switching windows at each comment. `pg_wal_replay_pause()` freezes the standby's replay, so the lag lasts as long as you like, and the result is the same every time.
Replace `0/5003FD0` with the `my_write` your leader printed. Before the first comparison on the standby, predict `received` and `replayed`: which one has passed your write?

code.title: psql on the standby and on the primary

try.expect:
On fresh servers, the refund is id 7 and `my_write` is `0/5003FD0` (yours may differ). The standby can't see it:

```text
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
(0 rows)

 replayed  | received  | has_my_write
-----------+-----------+--------------
 0/5000000 | 0/5004000 | f
(1 row)
```

The standby has received the log past your write (`0/5004000`) and applied none of it, because replay is paused. The comparison says `f` (false), so a router would send this read to the leader. Right after `pg_wal_replay_resume()`, the comparison can still say `f` for a moment, as it did in this run, because replay takes a few milliseconds to restart. A moment later, the refund is there:

```text
 has_my_write
--------------
 f
(1 row)

 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1200
(1 row)
```

That moment is why real code waits a limited time and checks again, rather than checking once. Leave the servers running for lesson 4, or stop them with `docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v`.

sections.h: Never going back in time: monotonic reads
sections.body:
A payment, pay-9, was authorized at 0 ms (the card's bank set the money aside) and captured at 1,000 ms (the money really moved). Someone on the company's support team keeps pay-9's page open and reloads it. Two followers answer, r1 20 ms behind and r2 900 ms behind, and the load balancer takes turns between them.

At 1,100 ms, r1 says captured. At 1,150 ms, r2 says authorized. At 1,200 ms, r1 says captured again. The capture appears, disappears and comes back. A support agent who acts on the second screen might capture the payment a second time.

In the club's terms, you read Tuesday's page in one town, then drive to the next town and find its copy still ends on Monday.

The agent changed nothing, so read-your-writes has nothing to say here. The missing promise is **monotonic reads**: once you've seen some state, your later reads never show an older one. Time may stand still for you, but it never runs backwards. It's weaker than "everyone sees the newest data", and stronger than eventual consistency.

The classic fix is sticky routing: send all of one user's reads to the same follower. The app picks it from a hash of the user's id, a number worked out from the id that always comes out the same for the same id. One follower's position only moves forward, so neither do the user's reads.

Sticky routing has two costs. Load is uneven when some users read much more than others. And it breaks exactly when you need it most: when the sticky follower dies, the user moves to another follower, which may be behind the first. The lab shows that case. A user sees captured on r1, r1 dies, and the next read, on r2, says authorized.

The precise fix is the last section's token, with one more rule. The session remembers the highest position any of its reads was served at, and the router never serves it below that, or below its own last write. The sticky follower is tried first, so most reads stay where they were. A dead or lagging one is skipped for any follower at or past the token, or for the leader. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions give monotonic reads this way, as part of the same promise that needs `majority` for reads and writes.

So far, every surprise came from one log read at two positions. Next, two logs.

try.title: Count the steps back in time
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the first command below. It reloads pay-9 six times, first taking turns between r1 and r2 (round robin), then routed with a session token.
The second command puts r2 only 40 ms behind. Before you run it: will round robin still go back in time? Why doesn't a smaller lag make the surprise impossible?
try.expect:
```text
round robin, no token:
   1100 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1150 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
   1200 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1250 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
   1300 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1350 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
  went back 3 times
with a session token (never below the highest position seen):
   1100 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1150 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1200 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1250 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1300 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1350 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
  went back 0 times
```

With the token, the session stays on its sticky follower, r1 here. It would use r2 only if r1 died, and only once r2 had reached position 2. With r2 40 ms behind, round robin also goes back 0 times, because these reloads start 100 ms after the capture, and both followers have it by then. A reload between 1,020 and 1,040 ms would still catch r2 without it. Any two followers at different positions can cause the surprise, and a smaller lag only makes the window narrower.

sections.h: Causes before effects: consistent prefix reads
sections.body:
Inside one leader's log, a follower always shows a prefix of history: everything up to its position, in order, and nothing after it. If the authorization of pay-1 is position 40 and its capture is position 41, no follower can show the capture without the authorization. Single-leader replication gives you this for free.

It stops being free when related writes go into different logs. When a dataset grows too big for one machine, the Partitioning track splits it into shards, pieces that each have their own leader, log and followers. Nothing orders shard 0's log against shard 1's.

Suppose the company puts authorizations on shard 0, and captures and refunds on shard 1. Payment number n is authorized at n × 50 ms and captured 30 ms later. Shard 0's follower is 400 ms behind, and shard 1's is 20 ms behind. At 100 ms, the fraud dashboard, a page that watches for suspicious payments, reads both followers. It sees pay-1 captured, with no authorization anywhere, and raises an alert. In the lab, 201 refreshes over two seconds count 700 such sightings.

The club picture shows why. The club now keeps two notebooks, one for authorizations and one for captures, posted separately. A town can get the captures notebook's new page days before the authorizations page it depends on.

The promise this needs is **consistent prefix reads**: if writes happened in a certain order, anyone who reads them sees them in that order, never an effect before its cause.

The fix is to keep writes that depend on each other in one log. Split the shards by payment id instead of by kind of event. Then a payment's authorization, capture and refund share one log, and any follower of that shard shows them in order. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, works the same way. Order holds only within one of its logs, called a partition. So you give each message the payment id as its key, and Kafka sends all of a payment's messages to one partition. (The Messaging track's lesson Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering covers it.)

That covers whatever shares the key. A shop's daily total, built from many payments on many shards, can still be read at a moment when some shards are ahead of others. The general fix is to track dependencies: each write carries the positions it depends on, one per shard, and a reader waits until its followers reach all of them. That's called causal consistency, and the Consistency and consensus track builds it.

| Surprise | What the user sees | Fix | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read-your-writes | their own change missing | a token of their last write, or the leader | some reads on the leader; a token per user |
| Monotonic reads | data going back in time | a sticky follower plus a highest-seen token | uneven load; rerouting |
| Consistent prefix | an effect before its cause | one log (one shard key) for related writes | choosing the key; order across keys still open |

The table also shows this lesson's limit. Each fix makes one user's view hang together, and none makes a follower show a change the moment it happens. Next, we'll run all of it on one real database.

try.title: Split by kind of event, then by payment
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the first command below. It writes 20 payments' authorizations and captures twice: once with one shard per kind of event, and once with shards split by payment id. Each time, it counts the captures the fraud dashboard sees without their authorization.
The second command puts both followers 20 ms behind. Predict the count. Is the problem the lag, or the two logs?
try.expect:
```text
a shard per event type (shard 0's follower 400 ms behind, shard 1's 20 ms):
  at 100 ms the dashboard shows pay-1 captured, with no authorization
  captures without an authorization, summed over 201 refreshes: 700
a shard per payment (shard 0's follower 400 ms behind, shard 1's 20 ms):
  no capture ever appears before its authorization
  captures without an authorization, summed over 201 refreshes: 0
```

Each of the 20 captures is visible for 350 ms before its authorization arrives, and the dashboard refreshes every 10 ms: 20 × 35 = 700. With `-Pargs='prefix 20'`, both lines say 0, because each capture is written 30 ms after its authorization and both followers are equally behind. Make the lags differ by more than 30 ms (`prefix 60` counts 20), and splitting by kind of event shows the surprise again. The cause is two logs copied separately; the lag only decides how often you see it.

compare.title: Read-your-writes on PostgreSQL and on MongoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL (JDBC, Kotlin)
a.title: carry the LSN yourself

b.label: MongoDB (Java sync driver, Kotlin)
b.title: the session carries it

compare.note: Both compare a log position with the follower's. With PostgreSQL, your code reads the position after the write, keeps it with the user's session and decides where to read, so you choose the wait and the fallback. MongoDB's driver, the library a program uses to talk to it, keeps the write's time in the session object, and the server does the waiting. But that works only within one session object: pass it between requests, or store the time and hand it to the next session with `advanceOperationTime`. And it works only with `majority` for reads and writes.

worked.title: A read router with a session token

steps.say: Keep the token with the user's session, not with a connection: one open connection to the database serves many users in turn. The token holds two positions: the user's last write, and the highest position any of the user's reads was served at.
After a commit, raise `lastWritten` to the commit's position. Any position that only grows with the log works: an LSN as a number, a count of MySQL transaction ids, a MongoDB operation time.
steps.code: fun afterWrite(t: ReadToken, commitPosition: Long) = t.copy(lastWritten = maxOf(t.lastWritten, commitPosition))

steps.say: Route: the sticky follower first, then any other at or past the floor, and the leader last. Count the reads that go to the leader; that number is what the promise costs you.
After the read, raise `lastSeen` to the position it was served at, so the next read can't go backwards.
steps.code: fun afterRead(t: ReadToken, servedAt: Long) = t.copy(lastSeen = maxOf(t.lastSeen, servedAt))

steps.say: Send the token to the browser, or store it for each user, and send it back with every request. For a phone and a laptop, store it on the server under the user's id; a cookie only covers one browser.
steps.code:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
X-Read-After: 83895248

GET /refunds?payment=pay-41 HTTP/1.1
X-Read-After: 83895248

lab.title: Cause the three surprises, then route around them
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder; they need no Docker. 14 of the 18 fail. The 4 that already pass are the bug reports: using only the given code, they show a missing refund, a payment page going back in time, sticky routing failing when it has to reroute, and 700 captures without an authorization. Read `Lag.kt`. A `Replica`'s position at any moment comes from the log and its lag, and `pause()` freezes it, like `pg_wal_replay_pause()`.

Exercise 1, `readYourWrites`: read on the offered follower if it has the session's last write, wait for it if that takes at most `maxWaitMs`, and otherwise go to the leader. `ReadYourWritesTest` includes a paused follower, and the support agent whose token is 0.

Exercise 2, `monotonicReads`: never serve a session below the larger of its last write and its highest read, and try the sticky follower first. `MonotonicReadsTest` reloads pay-9 ten times, and `SessionPropertyTest` throws 200 random histories of lags, pauses, writes and reads at it.
Exercise 3, `shardFor`: put every event of a payment in the same shard. `ConsistentPrefixTest` counts what the fraud dashboard sees: 700 with a shard per kind of event, and 0 with yours.
hints: `readYourWrites`: check `replica.alive`, then `replica.position(now) >= session.lastWritten`. If that fails, `replica.reaches(session.lastWritten)` is the moment it will be there, or null if it's paused below it; the wait is that moment minus `now`.

`monotonicReads`: `val token = maxOf(session.lastSeen, session.lastWritten)`. Build the order as `listOfNotNull(sticky) + replicas.filter { it.alive && it !== sticky }`, then `firstOrNull { it.position(now) >= token }`, and fall back to `Route(leader)`.
If the property test fails, jqwik (the library that runs the random tests) prints the seed and the lags. Replay that seed in a plain test, and print every `Read` it makes.

drill.title: Name the surprise and its fix
drill.prompt: Without looking, name the surprise in each case, then the fix and what it costs. (a) A customer changes their card's nickname, and the next page shows the old nickname. (b) A support agent sees a refund marked "sent", reloads, and sees "requested". (c) A page of checks shows a refund for a payment that has no capture yet. Then write the one-line check a PostgreSQL router runs before reading on a standby.

answer.src:
(a) read-your-writes violation
    fix: carry the LSN of the customer's last write; read on a standby only when
    pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN, else wait briefly or read the primary
    cost: some reads go to the primary; the token must follow the user across devices
(b) monotonic reads violation
    fix: sticky standby per user plus a token of the highest position already seen
    cost: uneven load; a dead sticky standby needs a reroute that respects the token
(c) consistent prefix violation (capture and refund on different shards or logs)
    fix: shard or key both by payment id so they share one ordered log
    cost: the key must group everything that has to stay ordered

check:  SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= :token::pg_lsn;

recap: Asynchronous followers lag, usually by milliseconds and sometimes by minutes, with no limit. Eventual consistency only promises that the copies agree once writes stop.
Each surprise is a read served at a position behind something the reader already did or saw. Each fix makes the reader carry a position and refuse to read below it.

Read-your-writes: keep the position of the user's last write (PostgreSQL's LSN, MySQL's GTID set, MongoDB's operation time) and read only from followers at or past it, with a limited wait and the leader as fallback. `remote_apply` makes every commit pay instead.
Monotonic reads: a session never reads older data than it has already seen. Sticky routing gives this until the sticky follower dies; a highest-seen position makes it survive the reroute.

Consistent prefix: one log gives it for free, and writes spread over shards lose it. Keep writes that depend on each other in one log (key by payment id), or track dependencies, which is causal consistency.
The limit: these fixes keep one user's view in order. None makes a follower show a change the moment it happens; that's linearizability, a far stronger promise.
closing:
We started with a café owner who refunded a coffee, saw no refund and tapped again. Her refund was on the leader all along. She read a follower that hadn't reached it, and the fix was to carry her last write's position and refuse to read below it.

Watch for the three surprises in apps you use: your own change missing after a reload, a list that loses an item and gets it back, a reply shown before the message it answers. On a PostgreSQL standby you can reach, `SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();` shows how far it has applied the log.

Next, we'll run this whole track on real PostgreSQL, and meet the one copy replication can't give you: a backup.

quiz.q: A shop owner changes the bank account her takings are paid into, on her phone. Then she opens her page on her laptop, which reads from followers. The app keeps the read-your-writes token in a browser cookie. What does the laptop show, and why?
options: The new account, because the token is tied to her user id
Possibly the old account: the laptop's browser has no token for the phone's change, so any follower qualifies
An error, because the laptop has no token at all
The new account, because read-your-writes covers every device a user has
quiz.why: The token lives where it was set, in the phone's browser. The laptop has token 0, so the router treats every follower as fresh enough. Read-your-writes across devices needs the token kept on the server, under the user's account. Nothing shows an error, which is why this bug survives testing on one device.

quiz.q: A PostgreSQL router checks `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= token` before it uses a standby. The standby's replay is paused for maintenance, but it's still receiving the log. What happens to a user who made a change a moment ago?
options: Their reads go to the standby, because it has received the log
Their reads wait until the maintenance ends
Their reads go to the leader (or wait, then fall back), because the replay position stays below their token
Their reads see the change, because the standby keeps applying the log even while replay is paused
quiz.why: Receiving the log isn't applying it. Reads on the standby see only data that was applied, and `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` stays where replay stopped. The router sees it's below the token and uses the leader. That's why the check uses the replay position, not the receive position, as the Try it showed.

quiz.q: An operations page sends each user's reads to the follower picked by a hash of their user id. Users never see data go backwards, until one follower is restarted. What do its users see, and what makes the fix survive that?
options: Nothing changes: sticky routing guarantees monotonic reads
Their reads move to another follower that may be behind the first; keeping the highest position each session has seen, and skipping followers below it, prevents the step back
They see an error until the follower is back
They see newer data, because the other followers are always ahead
quiz.why: Sticky routing works because one follower's position only grows. A reroute breaks that: the new follower can be behind, and the user's next read goes back in time, as the lab's test shows. A highest-seen position in the session lets the router skip followers below it and fall back to the leader.

quiz.q: Kafka keeps messages in logs called partitions. A stream of payment events uses the kind of event ("authorized", "captured") as its key, so authorizations and captures land in different partitions. A program builds a fraud view from both. What can it see?
options: A capture before its authorization, because order holds only within a partition
Nothing wrong, because Kafka keeps every write in order
Captures twice, because two partitions mean two copies
Missing authorizations, because it reads only one partition at a time
quiz.why: Each partition is its own log, and nothing orders one against the other, so the program can read the captures partition ahead of the authorizations partition. Using the payment id as the key puts a payment's events in one partition, in order: the consistent-prefix fix, in Kafka's terms.

quiz.q: In One leader, many followers, an asynchronous leader acknowledged a refund at position 812 and then died; the promoted follower had reached only 800. The shop owner's session token says 812. What does this lesson's router do for her next reads?
options: It reads from the new leader and shows the refund
It falls back to the new leader until positions pass 812 again with other writes, then shows a history without the refund: a token can't bring back a write the failover lost
It reads from the old leader, which still has position 812
It shows an error, because no machine has position 812
quiz.why: A token only makes a read wait for a write that exists in the surviving log. The failover lost 801 to 812, the new leader soon writes its own 801 to 812, every machine passes the token, and the refund is missing. Read-your-writes can't promise more than replication kept. That's why MongoDB ties its session promises to `majority` writes: a write on a majority survives the failover, so the token points at something that still exists.

flashcards.back: If writes stop, all copies end up with the same data, eventually. It puts no limit on how long that takes, or on what reads see meanwhile.

flashcards.front: Read-your-writes: what does it promise, and to whom?
flashcards.back: After you change something, your own reads always show the change. It says nothing about what other users see.

flashcards.front: On PostgreSQL, what is the read-your-writes check before using a standby?
flashcards.back: Read pg_current_wal_lsn() after the commit. Read on the standby only if pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN; otherwise wait briefly or use the leader.

flashcards.front: Monotonic reads: what does it forbid?
flashcards.back: Seeing an older state after you've seen a newer one, such as a captured payment shown as authorized on the next reload.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't sticky routing alone guarantee monotonic reads?
flashcards.back: When the sticky follower fails, the user moves to another follower that may be further behind. A token of the highest position seen closes that gap.

flashcards.front: When does consistent prefix come for free, and when not?
flashcards.back: Free within one leader's log, because followers apply it in order. Lost when related writes go to different shards or partitions, which have no order between them.

flashcards.front: What does MongoDB need for a causally consistent session's promises to hold?
flashcards.back: The majority setting for both reads and writes. The driver sends the session's operation time as afterClusterTime, and a follower waits until it has applied that far.

terms.plain: How far a follower is behind the leader, as a difference of log positions or as time.
The copies agree once writes stop, with no promise about when.
Your own reads always show your own earlier changes.
Once you've seen some data, you never see an older version of it.
Writes are seen in the order they happened, never an effect before its cause.
A log position the app carries for one user, so that the user's reads are never served below it.
Sending all of one user's reads to the same follower.

explain_back.prompt: A friend on a small team asks why "read from the copies to take load off the main database" caused three different kinds of bug reports, and why one fix covers two of them but not the third. Explain it.
explain_back.answer: The copies apply the main database's log a little later, so each one shows a moment in the past, and different copies show different moments. In the first bug, a shop owner makes a change and at once reads from a copy that hasn't got it yet, so her own change looks lost. In the second, someone reloads and lands on a copy that's further behind than the one they used before, so the data seems to go back in time. Both happen because a read was served from a point earlier than something the user had already done or seen. So one fix covers both: give the user a position in the log, the position of their last change and the newest position they've read at, and serve their reads only from copies that have reached it, otherwise from the main database. The third bug is different. The fraud dashboard shows a capture before its authorization because those two events live in different shards, each with its own log, and nothing orders one shard against another. A position in one log doesn't help there. The fix is to put events that depend on each other in the same log, by splitting the shards by payment id, or to track dependencies across shards, which is a bigger project.

deeper.body:
The four session guarantees come from a 1994 paper by Terry and colleagues on Bayou, a research database. They are read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, and monotonic writes. The last two are about writes. Monotonic writes says your writes are applied in the order you made them. Writes-follow-reads says a write you make after reading something is ordered after what you read. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions promise all four with the `majority` setting for reads and writes. Jepsen's map of consistency models shows where they sit: causal consistency includes all four, and all of them can stay available during a network split, as long as each client keeps talking to the same copies. Jepsen calls that sticky available.

Bounded staleness is a different deal. Instead of carrying a position, the client says "nothing older than 5 seconds". Azure Cosmos DB sells it as a consistency level. And DynamoDB's global tables, copies of one table in several regions, document that a strongly consistent read can be stale if the item was last written in another region. Time limits are easy to state and hard to check, because a follower's idea of its lag in seconds depends on clocks (the Faults, time and truth track covers why clocks are fragile).

PostgreSQL has a second kind of "the standby read waits": `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` with `synchronous_standby_names`, which makes the writer wait instead of the reader. A quorum of standbys, such as `ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)`, plus `remote_apply` makes any of those standbys safe to read from once the commit returns. That's close to the model Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 recommends when you can afford it, copies that are always up to date. Its warning is the one this lesson started from: pretending asynchronous copies are synchronous is where these bugs come from.
